summary: AstroVitals is an on-board health monitoring system for astronauts on missions too far from Earth for real-time medical support. It builds a personal baseline for each crew member, including their daily rhythm, and tracks heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, respiration, heart-rate variability, sleep and exercise. A drift advisory fires when someone moves away from their own normal while still inside textbook limits. Warnings and critical alerts fire when safe limits are crossed. Exercise widens the limits to avoid false alarms. Habitat sensors for CO₂, pressure and radiation feed the model, so alerts name a likely cause. Each alert gives a first action the crew can take immediately, and downlinks are queued with realistic light delay for low Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars.
details:
How it works: The system senses, analyses and acts. Wearable and habitat streams (simulated in this demo) feed an on-board engine. The engine learns each astronaut’s baseline and circadian rhythm. It raises a warning or critical alert after a reading stays outside safe limits for 3 minutes. It raises a drift advisory when a reading sits more than 3.5 standard deviations from that person’s own baseline while still in the normal range. During exercise and recovery, limits widen. Cabin CO₂ and pressure shift the expected vitals, so alerts say “likely linked to high cabin CO₂”. Warnings and critical alerts are queued to ground, and the reply time follows the light delay for the chosen destination (about 25 min round trip for Mars on average).

Tech stack: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG charts in a single file. No backend, so it can run offline on a spacecraft.

Creativity: personal-baseline drift detection, exercise-aware limits, habitat-to-vitals coupling, and light-delay-aware autonomy.

Impact: the crew gets decision support when ground help is minutes away. That matters for Moon and Mars missions, where a medical event can’t wait for a round trip.
